summary: 38b covers: 'from yours they give you' (divine provision for Temple); Hugras's vocal trill technique (thumb in mouth) and refusal to teach; interpretation of 'the name of the wicked shall rot' (R. Elazar: forgotten; R. Yochanan: preserved in infamy); R. Elazar's principle that blessing of the righteous and curse of the wicked are mirror images.

display.whats: 'And from yours they give you' - God provides what is needed for Temple service.
display.hint: Whatever skills are needed, God will provide them through those who possess them.
display.title: 'From Yours They Give You': Temple Provision Belongs to God

learning.ahaMoment: Temple service depends on God's provision: even withheld knowledge eventually becomes available.
learning.memoryAnchor: From yours - everything dedicated to the Temple comes from God; no one can permanently withhold.
learning.learnerQuestion: What does the teaching 'from yours they give you' add to the story of families withholding Temple skills?
learning.coreTension: Beth Avtinas and others believed their family knowledge was theirs to withhold, yet the Temple's resources, the Gemara teaches, ultimately come from God, not from any individual's private possession.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara frames the entire withheld-knowledge narrative through this principle: whatever serves the Temple was never truly owned by the families who held it.

takeaway.text: 'From yours they give you' teaches that no person can permanently withhold what belongs to Temple service, since the knowledge ultimately comes from God's provision.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may treat this teaching as a separate aphorism rather than seeing it as the Gemara's theological frame for the families-who-withheld narrative.

argumentFlow.label: Ruling: 'And from yours they give you' -
argumentFlow.text: 'And from yours they give you' - God provides; no person truly owns what belongs to Temple service.

misconceptions.misconception: When the Temple families refused to share their skills, this meant those skills were permanently lost.
misconceptions.correction: The Gemara teaches 'from yours they give you' - God provided the needed knowledge even when families withheld it. Divine providence filled the gap.

visualizableElements.description: From yours they give you - Temple resources ultimately come from God

quizSeeds.question: What does 'from yours they give you' teach about Temple service?
quizSeeds.answer: Whatever is used for Temple service ultimately comes from God; human beings cannot permanently withhold what God has designated for sacred use.

sugyot.finalRuling: 'From yours they give you' - God provides all that is needed for the Temple service.

display.whats: Hugras ben Levi's voice technique for Temple music; a negative tradition.
display.hint: Hugras could hit the musical note with his thumb in his mouth; his descendants kept this secret too.
display.title: Hugras's Lost Vocal Trill

learning.ahaMoment: Hugras's vocal artistry was extraordinary but his secrecy was criticized; the voice and knowledge both perished with him.
learning.memoryAnchor: Thumb in mouth = Hugras's secret trill; never shared; lost with his death.
learning.learnerQuestion: What was Hugras ben Levi's secret technique, and why does the Gemara record it negatively despite its skill?
learning.coreTension: Hugras's thumb-in-mouth vocal trill was an extraordinary skill for Temple song, yet extraordinary skill did not exempt him, or his descendants, from the same shame applied to the other secret-keeping families.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara describes the technique in detail, then notes that he and his descendants kept it secret until it was lost entirely, illustrating that skill without teaching still earns the Mishna's censure.

takeaway.text: Hugras ben Levi's vocal trill technique was extraordinary, but his refusal to teach it, continued by his descendants, meant the skill was lost and his family is remembered for shame, not praise.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may assume the detailed, admiring description of the technique signals approval, missing that the Gemara pairs technical praise with moral censure.

argumentFlow.label: Elaboration: Hugras ben Levi had a special vocal
argumentFlow.text: Hugras ben Levi had a special vocal technique: thumb in mouth for a trill during Temple songs.

argumentFlow.label: Ruling: He refused to teach it; his descendants
argumentFlow.text: He refused to teach it; his descendants also kept it secret; the technique was lost.

misconceptions.misconception: Hugras ben Levi's vocal technique was widely celebrated and is described positively in the Talmud.
misconceptions.correction: His technique was extraordinary but his secrecy was criticized. The Gemara preserves his memory alongside a negative judgment - extraordinary skill does not excuse knowledge-hoarding.

quizSeeds.question: What was Hugras ben Levi's secret technique?
quizSeeds.answer: He placed his thumb in his mouth to produce a special trill or resonance for Levitical Temple music.

sugyot.finalRuling: Hugras's vocal trill (thumb in mouth) was extraordinary but never taught; lost at his death.

display.whats: The name of the wicked rots (Prov. 10:7); positive vs negative Temple family legacies.
display.hint: R. Elazar: the name of the wicked is forgotten; R. Yochanan: their deeds live on in infamy.
display.title: 'The Name of the Wicked Shall Rot': Forgotten or Shamed?

learning.ahaMoment: Memory cuts both ways: the righteous are remembered for blessing; the wicked for shame. Temple legacy is permanent.
learning.memoryAnchor: Name rots = either forgotten or remembered in shame - either way, no honor. Temple shame endures.
learning.learnerQuestion: Does Proverbs 10:7's 'the name of the wicked shall rot' mean their name disappears, or that it persists as a mark of shame?
learning.coreTension: R. Elazar reads 'rot' as forgetting, while R. Yochanan reads it as persisting in infamy, two opposite outcomes from the same verse, both called 'rot.'
learning.coreMove: The Gemara resolves the dispute using the Mishna itself as proof: since Beth Garmu and the other families are named explicitly for shame, their names were not forgotten, supporting R. Yochanan's reading.

takeaway.text: The Mishna's explicit naming of shamed families serves as proof for R. Yochanan: 'the name of the wicked shall rot' means the name endures in infamy, not that it is forgotten.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may assume 'rot' straightforwardly means disappearance, missing how the Gemara uses the Mishna's preserved names as textual evidence against that reading.

misconceptions.misconception: 'The name of the wicked rots' means these families are simply forgotten.
misconceptions.correction: It means their names are actively preserved - in infamy. The Talmud records their names precisely so their shame is eternal, the inverse of the righteous who are remembered for blessing.

quizSeeds.answer: Their name is preserved in infamy - they are remembered in shame, not forgotten.

sugyot.finalRuling: The name of the wicked endures in shame; the righteous are blessed even after death - both legacies are permanent.

display.whats: From the blessing of the righteous one can learn about the curse of the wicked, and vice versa.
display.hint: The contrasting memories of Temple families teach about divine reward and punishment.
display.title: Blessing of the Righteous, Curse of the Wicked: Mirror Principles

learning.ahaMoment: One lesson teaches two: bless the righteous by contrasting with the wicked, curse the wicked by contrasting with the righteous.
learning.memoryAnchor: Mirror image: righteous = blessing (learn from it the curse of the wicked); wicked = shame (learn the blessing of the righteous).
learning.learnerQuestion: Why does R. Elazar say the blessing of the righteous and the curse of the wicked can each be learned from the other?
learning.coreTension: The Mishna records both praised families (Ben Katin, Queen Helene) and shamed families (Beth Garmu) in the same list, raising the question of whether these are two separate lessons or one principle running in both directions.
learning.coreMove: R. Elazar derives that the two are mirror images: the qualities that earn blessing, sharing freely, are the inverse of the qualities that earn curse, withholding, so each illuminates the other from a single textual contrast.

takeaway.text: R. Elazar's principle: from the blessing of the righteous you can derive the nature of the wicked's curse, and vice versa, since the Mishna's praised and shamed families are mirror images of the same behavior.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may treat the Mishna's two lists as unrelated examples rather than seeing R. Elazar's point that they function as a single mirrored teaching.

misconceptions.misconception: The contrast between blessing the righteous and cursing the wicked requires two separate scriptural sources.
misconceptions.correction: The Gemara teaches that one verse teaches both: from the blessing of the righteous you can derive the curse of the wicked, and vice versa - a single textual principle cuts both ways.

quizSeeds.answer: From the blessing of the righteous you can understand the nature of the wicked's curse, and vice versa - they are mirror images.

sugyot.finalRuling: From the blessing of the righteous you learn the nature of the wicked's punishment; their legacies are mirror images.

rashiTranslations.en: Rashi: opens 'and from what is yours they will give you' - meaning it is not a gift from their own, but rather a fixed sustenance
Rashi: continues - given you from Heaven. Then opens 'and no kingdom touches its fellow's own' - once the time for the kingdom
Rashi: continues - to fall arrives, and another rises, it does not delay even a hairsbreadth, but whichever kingdom's time is to fall
Rashi: continues - at night falls at night, as it is stated (Daniel 5): 'in that night Belshazzar was slain,'
Rashi: continues - and whichever kingdom's time is by day falls by day, as it is stated
Rashi: concludes - (Ezekiel 30): 'and at Tachpanches the day grew dark.'
Rashi: opens 'between the folds' - between the split of the lip's own
Rashi: continues - flesh opposite the partition of the nose. Then opens 'they would recoil with a sudden'
Rashi: concludes - jerk of the head - they would startle at the strength of the sound.
Rashi: opens 'rakvivut' - rust, like a rusted iron
Rashi: continues - vessel that is no longer used. Then opens 'since we do not'
Rashi: continues - name children after them' - a person should not name his son a wicked
Rashi: continues - man's name. Then opens 'she measured him in handbreadths' -
Rashi: concludes - to know how much he grew from day to day, and gave the weight equal to the growth.
Rashi: opens 'a priest and a prophet' - Zecharia ben Yehoyada the priest, so it seems that we do
Rashi: continues - name children after the wicked, since Doeg the Edomite was wicked
Rashi: continues - and this one named his child after him. Then opens 'see what became'
Rashi: continues - of him - see what happened
Rashi: concludes - to him, that he was slaughtered.
Rashi: opens 'a righteous person of his own accord' - through
Rashi: continues - his own deeds is remembered for good, 'a wicked person also through
Rashi: concludes - his fellow' - is remembered for evil. Then opens 'the name of the wicked' -
Rashi: concludes - and it does not say 'the wicked one' in the singular. Then opens 'I who conceal'
Rashi: continues - from Abraham' - and since He mentioned his own name, He blessed him,
Rashi: concludes - and immediately adjacent: 'and Abraham shall surely become,' etc.
Rashi: opens 'Ovadia' - who dwelled between Achav and Izevel.
Rashi: opens 'from the blessing of the righteous, etc.' - in the place
Rashi: continues - where the Holy One blesses the righteous, there
Rashi: concludes - He curses the wicked. Then opens 'and He saw the light' -
Rashi: continues - He saw in His own mind that the world's light would endure
Rashi: concludes - for the sake of the righteous one, who is good. Then opens 'and He set'
Rashi: continues - upon them the world' - He scattered them through all the generations,
Rashi: concludes - to be the foundation and support and pillar sustaining the world.
Rashi: opens 'the feet of His pious ones' -
Rashi: continues - for the sake of His pious ones, like 'the Lord has blessed you for my sake' (Genesis
Rashi: continues - 30). Then opens 'he no longer sins,' as it is stated 'the feet of His pious ones'
Rashi: continues - He shall guard - He guards the very end of His pious ones. Then opens 'a first
Rashi: continues - time and a second time,' etc. - 'the feet of His pious ones'
Rashi: continues - once he has conducted himself in kindness twice, like this
Rashi: continues - phrase 'three regalim' (Numbers 22), twice He guards
Rashi: concludes - him from sin. Then opens 'once a person comes to defile himself' -
Rashi: continues - to become wicked. Then opens 'they open for him' - an opening
Rashi: continues - for impurity to enter him, they facilitate it in his hand
Rashi: concludes - and they do not withhold from him, from Heaven, to stop him.
Rashi: opens 'if it is for scoffers, he scoffs' - if it is for scoffers
Rashi: continues - he comes to join, He shall scoff - they neither withhold from him
Rashi: continues - nor help him. Then opens 'if for the humble' - he comes
Rashi: concludes - to join, He shall grant favor to whoever it is in His power to grant.

Rashi: the daf's final truncated word - 'came,' the start of the dibbur hamatchil in Rabbi Yishmael's own school parable about a merchant of naphtha and balsam, whose text continues on 39a. Per the established boundary convention, this entry is anchored to the daf's own final locally captured Gemara line even though the DH's own point is itself still open at the point of truncation.
